We compare quantitative ratings from 6 frontier LLMs (GPT-5 Pro, GPT-5.2 Pro, GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.0 Flash) against human expert reviews from [The Unjournal](https://unjournal.pubpub.org). Across all models, 45 papers have both human and LLM evaluations. Agreement metrics and Krippendorff's alpha below are computed on the 33-paper matched sample with Claude Opus 4.6 evaluations, so that all models are compared on identical papers.

We submit each PDF through a single, schema-enforced API call. The system prompt mirrors The Unjournal rubric, blocks extrinsic priors (authors, venue, web context), and requires strict JSON: a ~1k-word diagnostic summary plus numeric midpoints and 90% credible intervals for every metric.^[0–100 percentiles relative to a reference group of ~'all serious work you have read in this area in the last three years', overall (global quality/impact), claims_evidence (claim clarity/support), methods (design/identification/robustness), advancing_knowledge (contribution to field/practice), logic_communication (internal consistency and exposition), open_science (reproducibility, data/code availability), and global_relevance (decision and priority usefulness). Journal tiers: (0–5, continuous) capture where the work should publish vs. will publish.] Each numeric field carries a midpoint (model's 50% belief) and a 90% credible interval; wide intervals indicate acknowledged uncertainty.

**Cost and token usage.** Token costs are computed from API-reported input/output tokens (GPT-5 Pro runs with `reasoning` = high).

Total cost across all 255 LLM evaluations: **$160.03**. Reasoning-capable models (GPT-5 Pro, GPT-5.2 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6) cost substantially more per paper than their lighter counterparts (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash), raising practical questions about cost-quality trade-offs for deployment at scale.





**Agreement metrics.** We assess agreement using Spearman *ρ* (rank-based, robust to outliers), MAE in percentile points (directly interpretable), RMSE, mean bias (LLM − Human; positive = LLM rates higher), and Pearson *r* for completeness. Full definitions appear in [Methods](methods.qmd). The **Human–Human** row in each table provides the empirical ceiling.


::: {#tbl-agreement .cell tbl-cap='Agreement between each LLM and human mean overall rating, matched sample (N = `r n_opus`). **Human–Human** row (top, bold) shows pairwise evaluator agreement on the same papers as an empirical upper bound. Spearman *ρ* (rank-based, robust to outliers) and MAE (in percentile points, directly interpretable) are primary metrics; Pearson *r* is shown for completeness. Bias = LLM − Human (positive = LLM more generous). Models sorted by Spearman *ρ*.'}

@tbl-agreement reports agreement metrics between each LLM and the human mean overall rating, with the Human–Human baseline as the top row. The Human–Human row shows pairwise correlation between the two evaluators assigned to the same paper: this is the empirical ceiling any model can hope to reach, since the human "mean" used as the reference is itself a noisy estimate. Where an LLM's Spearman *ρ* approaches the Human–Human baseline, it is providing signal comparable to an additional expert rater. Positive mean bias indicates the model rates papers higher than humans on average; negative bias indicates harsher ratings.

**Human baseline context.** Human percentile ratings are a noisy reference signal, not ground truth: even expert evaluators given the same paper differ systematically, reflecting genuine uncertainty in what a "correct" score would be. @tbl-human-baseline quantifies this noise as Krippendorff's α~HH~. The α~HL~ columns show how close each LLM comes to that ceiling. A model achieving α~HL~ ≥ α~HH~ on a criterion is generating signal indistinguishable from an additional human evaluator. Criteria where α~HH~ is already low indicate genuine expert disagreement; low α~HL~ on those criteria is therefore expected, not a model failure.


::: {#tbl-human-baseline .cell tbl-cap='Krippendorff\'s α~HH~ (inter-human agreement, **bold**) vs α~HL~ (human–LLM agreement) by criterion, matched sample (N = `r n_opus` papers). α~HH~ is the empirical ceiling: an LLM with α~HL~ ≥ α~HH~ performs at or above the human inter-rater level for that criterion. Criteria where α~HH~ is already low indicate genuine evaluator disagreement.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}

Where α~HL~ ≥ α~HH~, the LLM is performing at or above the ceiling set by human inter-rater variability — its ratings are as consistent with the human reference as a second human evaluator would be. Criteria where α~HH~ is already low (indicating genuine evaluator disagreement) naturally cap how well any model can do, and low α~HL~ on those criteria reflects the difficulty of the task rather than a model failure. Extended agreement analysis — including CI coverage, bootstrap confidence intervals, and mutual information — is available in the supplementary material.

**Criteria-level patterns.** @fig-criteria-heatmap displays the mean rating each evaluator type assigns across the seven criteria. Criteria where all models and humans converge (similar colour intensity) suggest robust agreement on that dimension; criteria with divergent columns indicate systematic differences in how humans and LLMs weigh that aspect of quality.


::: {.cell}

Criteria where all rows show similar colour intensity indicate broad agreement; divergent columns flag criteria-level systematic differences.](results_ratings_files/figure-pdf/fig-criteria-heatmap-1.pdf){#fig-criteria-heatmap}
:::

**Additional models.** @fig-scatter-other shows overall ratings for the two lightweight models---GPT-4o-mini and Gemini 2.0 Flash---against human mean ratings. These models cost 50--200× less per paper than reasoning-capable models (see @tbl-cost-overview) but may sacrifice rating accuracy.


::: {.cell}
